newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. envoy in Uganda to press for Zaire ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy in Uganda to press for Zaire ceasefire.

text.p: U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni met on Friday in northern Uganda for talks on Zaire's spreading war.

Hope Kivengere, senior media aide to Museveni, told Reuters by telephone from Kampala that Sahnoun arrived in the northern outpost of Gulu and went straight into talks with Museveni, a former rebel leader.
"They have just started talks on the Zaire situation. I expect Sahnoun to leave straight after the talks" she said.
She said Museveni earlier met European Union envoy Aldo Ajello as diplomatic activity over the Zaire crisis gathered pace while President Mobutu Sese Seko headed back to Kinshasa from France.

The international community is banking on Museveni's influence in the region to push Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila into a ceasefire which he has so far rejected, saying a truce can only follow direct negotiations with Mobutu.
Sahnoun, a joint envoy of the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity, is expected to head on from Gulu to the Zairean rebel-held city of Kisangani for talks with Kabila.
Kabila arrived in Kisangani earlier on Friday for the first time since its capture last Saturday and received a hero's welcome from more than 10,000 residents.
On Thursday last week, Sahnoun met Museveni and Kabila in Gulu and the rebel leader rejected a plea for a ceasefire.

A diplomat said talks with Museveni and Kabila would centre on securing a ceasefire and would examine Mobutu's announcement through his son and spokesman that he does not rule out talks with the rebels.
Mobutu, who left hospital in Monaco on Wednesday after fresh cancer treatment, called on Thursday for a truce in a statement and for a Zairean national council to find a peace settlement.
Kabila ruled out a ceasefire before negotiations when he arrived in Kisangani. "We negotiate first," he told reporters.

Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) has seized more than one-fifth of Zaire since October. Kabila says he wants only face-to-face talks with Mobutu or his representative to decide how he will stand down.
Mobutu's son, Nzanga, said in France on Thursday that his father no longer ruled out talks with the rebels but wanted to involve the government, army and transitional parliament.

Mobutu, 66, has spent almost all his time in Europe since having prostate cancer surgery in August. He has dominated Zaire with a mix of political acumen and military ruthlessness since seizing power in 1965.
Diplomats said, depending on the outcome of talks with Museveni and Kabila, Sahnoun might take his diplomatic shuttle to Kinshasa where Mobutu is expected to arrive on Friday.

The rebel force is dominated by ethnic Tutsis, some of them Zairean Banyamulenge Tutsis and others said by intelligence sources to be members of Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army. The Rwandan government denies any involvement with the rebels.
Demobilised Ugandan troops, hired on contract, are also part of the rebel force. Kabila is a Zairean non-Tutsi from Shaba and his field commanders are a mixture of Zaireans and foreigners.
